name: Fonterra Shareholders' Fund
structural_note: FSF.NZ is NOT an operating company. It is a NZ managed investment scheme (unit trust) whose sole asset is a pool of 'Economic Rights' referable to shares in Fonterra Co-operative Group Limited (the actual dairy business). Unit holders receive the same dividends/distributions and capital returns per unit as a Fonterra farmer-shareholder receives per share, and the units revalue with the underlying Fonterra share price, but unit holders have NO voting rights and NO governance role in Fonterra. All financial commentary about 'the company's' revenue, margins, competitors, and strategy in this report describes Fonterra Co-operative Group Limited, whose performance the Fund's value is a direct look-through of.
overview: Fonterra Shareholders' Fund is a unit trust listed on the NZX Main Board (delisted from the ASX in February 2025) that gives investors who cannot hold Fonterra farmer shares (i.e. non-supplying investors, including the public) economic exposure to Fonterra Co-operative Group Limited -- New Zealand's dominant dairy co-operative and the world's largest dairy exporter, collecting roughly 80-85% of NZ's milk supply from ~8,000 farmer-shareholders. Following the completion of the ~NZ$4.22 billion sale of its global Consumer business (the Mainland Group -- Anchor, Mainland, Kapiti, Perfect Italiano, Western Star and related brands, excluding Greater China consumer) to Lactalis on 31 March 2026, Fonterra is now a more focused NZ milk-processing co-operative built around two segments: Ingredients (dairy commodity powders, proteins, fats sold largely via Global Dairy Trade-referenced pricing) and Foodservice (UHT cream, butter, mozzarella and other food-service inputs sold mainly into Greater China and Southeast Asian foodservice/bakery channels). The Fund itself holds no operating assets, has no employees, and is managed by FSF Management Company Limited, a small board with three unit-holder-elected independent directors and two directors appointed by Fonterra.

business_model.summary: The Fund's 'business model' is entirely a pass-through: it holds Economic Rights over Fonterra shares purchased from farmer-shareholders who choose to move some of their shareholding's economic (non-voting) rights into the Fund in exchange for cash, and it issues/redeems units against that pool. Fund unit holders receive the identical per-share dividends, capital returns and (via revaluation) the identical mark-to-market change in value as a Fonterra share, but hold no vote at Fonterra's co-operative AGM/board elections. Historically (Trading Among Farmers, 2012-2023) the Fund's unit price and Fonterra's internal farmer share price were linked via an arbitrage mechanism and a symmetric flexibility structure (farmers could move rights in and out of the Fund, subject to a Fund-size cap). Since Fonterra's move to 'Flexible Shareholding' (effective March 2023), the Fund unit price and the (now unlisted, farmer-only-traded) Fonterra share price have been formally DE-LINKED -- FSF Management confirmed in FY2024 that the Fund unit buy-out formula was amended to reference only the Fund's own unit VWAP rather than 50% Fonterra internal share VWAP, reflecting that Trading Among Farmers has been permanently retired.

revenue_streams.name: Ingredients (Fonterra segment -- look-through)
revenue_streams.trend: largest profit contributor; FY2025 operating profit ~NZ$1,017m (+17%), driven by protein demand, indexed/hedged pricing

revenue_streams.name: Foodservice (Fonterra segment -- look-through)
revenue_streams.trend: growing strongly, Greater China/SE Asia UHT cream, butter, mozzarella; Q3 FY2026 underlying operating profit +143% YoY to NZ$516m

revenue_streams.name: Consumer / Mainland Group (divested)
revenue_streams.trend: sold to Lactalis, completed 31-Mar-2026; no longer part of continuing operations from FY2026 onward (Greater China consumer/Anchor brand retained)

business_model.customer_type: Fund unit holders are retail/institutional investors (B2C from a market perspective); the underlying Fonterra business is B2B, selling dairy ingredients and foodservice inputs to food manufacturers, foodservice operators and distributors globally, with farmer-suppliers as Fonterra's other core 'customer' relationship (via milk collection and the Farmgate Milk Price).
business_model.geographic_mix: Milk collected entirely in New Zealand (~1.5-1.6bn kgMS/season); products exported globally with Greater China (~one-third of NZ dairy export volume) and Southeast Asia the dominant demand centres for Foodservice growth; Ingredients sold into global commodity markets referenced to Global Dairy Trade (GDT) auction pricing.
business_model.distribution_mechanism: Units traded on NZX Main Board under ticker FSF (ASX secondary listing voluntarily delisted ~27 Feb 2025 to consolidate liquidity and cut compliance costs). Distributions (dividends and any special/capital returns) are paid via a Custodian that can apply Fonterra's imputation credits to offset PIE tax before distribution to unit holders, following Fonterra's move to a tax-paying position from FY2025 (NZ tax losses exhausted).

fund_structure.trading_among_farmers_history: TAF was implemented in 2012 to remove Fonterra's obligation to issue/redeem farmer shares on demand (which had created up to NZ$600m of redemption-risk liquidity requirements). It created (a) a restricted farmer-only share market and (b) the Fund, allowing non-farmers to buy Economic Rights. Farmers could sell economic rights into the Fund (increasing Fund size) or buy them back out (decreasing Fund size), subject to a cap on Fund size relative to total Fonterra shares on issue -- originally up to ~20%.
fund_structure.flexible_shareholding_2023: Following a capital structure review (farmer mandate >85% in Dec-2021, NZ Government conditions attached given Fonterra's co-operative/DIRA status), Fonterra implemented 'Flexible Shareholding' in late March 2023, replacing TAF. Key changes: minimum farmer shareholding cut from 1 share per 1kg milksolids supplied to 1 share per 3kg (easier entry/retention for farmers); maximum raised from 2 shares/kg to 4 shares/kg; and the Fund-size cap was REDUCED from ~20% to 10% of total shares on issue, with the farmer share market becoming a more restricted, farmers-only venue. The Fund unit price is now formally de-linked from the (unlisted) internal farmer share price.
fund_structure.current_fund_size: As of April 2026, ~107.4 million FSF units on issue; market capitalisation approximately NZ$899 million as of 31 July 2026 (unit price ~NZ$6.90-8.30 range through 2026), representing roughly 6-10% of total Fonterra shares -- i.e. operating near or below the post-2023 cap.
fund_structure.delisting_wind_up_status: The Fund voluntarily delisted from the ASX (effective ~27 Feb 2025) to consolidate trading on NZX only, reducing dual-listing compliance costs -- this was a listing consolidation, NOT a wind-up. Separately, Fonterra's Board/chair (Peter McBride) has publicly stated the co-operative has 'no appetite at this stage' to wind up the Fund entirely. As of the most recent information available (mid-2026), FSF remains actively listed and trading on the NZX Main Board under ticker FSF; no wind-up, buyout, or delisting-from-NZX transaction has been announced or completed. This should be treated as a live, monitorable risk given Fonterra's broader capital structure simplification agenda (Flexible Shareholding, reduced Fund cap, Mainland divestment) -- the direction of travel has consistently been to shrink/marginalise the Fund's relative size, even though full wind-up has been explicitly ruled out for now.

main_competitors: Lactalis (France, now also a NZ/Australia consumer competitor via the acquired Mainland brands)
Dairy Farmers of America / US ingredients exporters
competitive_position.market_position: Dominant NZ milk processor collecting roughly 80-85% of New Zealand's total milk supply from its ~8,000 farmer-shareholders, making it the world's largest dairy exporter by volume and the reference-price setter via the Global Dairy Trade (GDT) auction platform it operates. Post-Mainland divestment, Fonterra is positioning itself as a more focused B2B Ingredients and Foodservice supplier rather than a global consumer branded-goods company.
competitive_position.market_share: ~80-85% of NZ milk collection (near-monopsony on the supply side domestically); globally a top-tier but not dominant player in dairy ingredients/foodservice against much larger diversified multinational dairy/food groups.

moat_factors.description: Co-operative structure and processing/logistics network give Fonterra a near-monopsony position over NZ milk supply, the cheapest pasture-based milk production in the world, underpinning cost-competitive commodity exports.

Fonterra operates and is the largest seller on GDT, the reference price mechanism for global dairy commodities, giving pricing transparency/influence advantages, though this is also a source of margin volatility.
Decade-plus foodservice distribution network and manufacturing presence (Anchor Food Professionals) in China/SE Asia bakery and QSR channels, difficult for new entrants to replicate quickly.

Farmer-ownership model secures reliable milk volumes without needing to compete on open-market milk-purchase prices in the way non-co-op processors sometimes must, but also constrains capital allocation flexibility (see weaknesses).

weaknesses: Co-operative governance structurally prioritises maximising the Farmgate Milk Price paid TO farmer-suppliers, which is a direct cost line that compresses group operating earnings -- a structural conflict of interest for Fund unit holders who benefit from higher earnings/dividends, not higher milk prices.
Now a pure commodity/B2B ingredients-and-foodservice business post-Mainland sale, with less earnings diversification and no owned global consumer brand portfolio to smooth commodity price cycles.
Historically volatile execution record (FY2018 guidance miss, Beingmate and Danone-related impairments, Foodservice China margin swings) reflecting exposure to GDT price swings and FX.
Fund unit holders have zero voting influence over Fonterra's capital allocation, milk price setting, or strategic decisions (including the future of the Fund itself).

growth_drivers: Post-divestment focus and capital redeployment into higher-margin Foodservice (UHT cream, butter, mozzarella) and advanced/protein Ingredients, targeting a return to FY23-level group earnings within roughly three years of the FY2026 Mainland divestment per CEO commentary
Continued volume and margin growth in Greater China and Southeast Asia foodservice channels (Q3 FY2026 Foodservice underlying operating profit +143% YoY to NZ$516m)
New manufacturing capacity investment: Edendale UHT cream and Studholme proteins facilities, plus further butter and cream-cheese capacity

Substantial debt reduction and balance sheet strength (net debt down to NZ$4.9bn at 1H FY2026 from NZ$5.5bn; adjusted net debt/EBITDA around 1.1x) supporting an 80%-of-earnings dividend payout policy (top of Fonterra's payout range) and capacity for further capital returns/buybacks

One-off tax-free NZ$2.00/unit capital return from Mainland sale proceeds paid 14 April 2026 (~NZ$3.2bn group-wide), demonstrating capital-return capability and providing a re-rating catalyst for the leaner, more focused entity
Return on capital target range of 10-12% from FY26 (tracking at 11.2% at 1H FY2026), above Fonterra's 5-year historical average, aided by the simplified balance sheet
New CEO (Richard Allen, succeeding Miles Hurrell from ~September 2026) framed publicly as leading Fonterra's 'next growth phase' post-restructure

business.risk: No governance rights / structural conflict of interest
business.description: Fund unit holders have no vote at Fonterra; the co-operative board and farmer-shareholders control the Farmgate Milk Price, which directly trades off against group profitability and unit-holder returns. There is no mechanism for unit holders to influence this.

Post-divestment, Fonterra's earnings are more concentrated in commodity Ingredients and Foodservice, both more exposed to GDT price and China demand swings than the divested branded consumer portfolio was.

Greater China represents roughly one-third of NZ dairy export volume and is the primary growth engine for Foodservice; any Chinese economic slowdown, local dairy oversupply, or geopolitical trade friction would disproportionately hit Fonterra's growth segment.

business.risk: Fund cap / relative size shrinkage and liquidity
business.description: The Fund-size cap was cut from ~20% to 10% under Flexible Shareholding, and the co-op's broader direction has been to reduce reliance on non-farmer capital; while a full wind-up has been explicitly ruled out for now, the trend of shrinking relative fund size and the 2025 ASX delisting both reduce potential liquidity for unit holders over time.

FSF Management has already amended contractual mechanics (2024 buy-out formula change) as TAF was retired; further restructuring of the Fund's terms, or a future decision to wind it up despite current management comments, cannot be ruled out given Fonterra's ongoing capital-structure simplification agenda.

financial.description: A high Farmgate Milk Price (good for farmer suppliers) mechanically compresses Fonterra's Ingredients margins and group operating profit (evident in FY2026 1H commentary: 'higher milk input costs compressed margins'); conversely low milk prices boost group earnings but signal weak dairy markets generally.
GDT auction pricing and NZD/USD and NZD/RMB exchange rates drive material swings in reported revenue and margins each period.

Fonterra exhausted NZ tax losses from FY2025 and began generating imputation credits; while broadly neutral/beneficial to unit holders via imputation credit pass-through, it permanently reduced headline after-tax EPS versus the tax-loss-shielded years.

regulatory.description: The NZ Government attached conditions to its support for the Flexible Shareholding capital restructure and continues to regulate Fonterra's near-monopsony position over NZ milk collection (Dairy Industry Restructuring Act); any future regulatory tightening or loosening directly affects Fund economics without unit holder input.

The prior Government's plan to price agricultural emissions from 2025 was pushed back and then scrapped by the current Coalition Government; Fonterra continues a voluntary emissions-differentiated payment scheme (1-5 NZc/kgMS from June 2025) rather than facing a mandated carbon cost, but policy could reverse under a future government, raising farmer input costs and indirectly Fonterra's milk supply economics.

regulatory.risk: Lactalis divestment conditions / ongoing supply agreements
regulatory.description: The Mainland sale included minimum-term raw milk (10 years) and ingredients (6 years) supply agreements to Lactalis; execution or renegotiation risk on these agreements is low but not zero.

macro.description: Global milk supply growth (noted by outgoing CEO Hurrell as a live FY2026 risk) and demand-side softness can pressure GDT prices and Fonterra margins simultaneously.

Drought or adverse weather in NZ dairying regions directly affects milk collection volumes, a key top-line driver referenced each period (e.g., 1H FY2026 milk collections +4% to 1,565m kgMS is itself a favourable/unfavourable swing factor).
FY2026 outlook commentary specifically flagged Middle East conflict-related shipping disruption and input cost inflation risk to guidance.

macro_factors.industry_outlook: Global dairy demand, especially in Asia, continues to grow structurally (protein/functional foods, foodservice/bakery penetration in China and SE Asia), but the industry remains a volatile, cyclical commodity business at the Ingredients level, priced off the Global Dairy Trade auction.
macro_factors.cyclicality: High at the commodity/GDT level (Ingredients); more resilient/growing at the Foodservice level, which is now a larger relative share of Fonterra's profit mix post-Mainland divestment.
macro_factors.interest_rate_sensitivity: Moderate — Fonterra carries several billion NZD of net debt (NZ$4.9bn at 1H FY2026) used partly to fund working capital swings tied to the milk payment cycle; lower rates reduce funding costs and support dividend capacity.
macro_factors.currency_exposure: High — NZD/USD and NZD/RMB movements materially affect reported export revenue and margins; a stronger NZD is a headwind to reported earnings.
key_input_costs: Raw milk (Farmgate Milk Price paid to farmer-suppliers — the single largest cost line)

recent_developments.event: Fonterra announced agreement to sell its global Consumer and associated businesses (Mainland Group: Anchor, Mainland, Kapiti, Perfect Italiano, Western Star, and NZ/Australia consumer operations, excluding Greater China consumer/Anchor brand) to Lactalis for NZ$4.22 billion (initially reported as ~$3.845bn headline enterprise value, finalised at $4.22bn).
Fonterra farmer shareholders voted to approve the Mainland Group divestment to Lactalis.
Regulatory approvals for the Lactalis transaction obtained; sale completion proceeded.

Fonterra CEO Miles Hurrell announced his resignation after eight years in the role (25-year Fonterra career); Richard Allen named as successor CEO, with Hurrell remaining in an advisory capacity through approximately September 2026 for transition.

Fonterra reported HY26 (six months to 31 January 2026) results: revenue NZ$13.9bn (+NZ$1.3bn), operating profit NZ$1,231m (up from NZ$1,107m), profit after tax NZ$750m (+3%); interim dividend raised to 24 cents/share plus a special Mainland dividend of 16 cents/share (100% of Mainland's FY26 earnings while under Fonterra ownership) = 40 cents total interim distribution; FY26 forecast Farmgate Milk Price range lifted to $9.40-$10.00/kgMS (midpoint $9.70, up from $9.50); FY26 earnings guidance raised to 50-65 cents/share from 45-65 cents; net debt reduced to NZ$4.9bn from NZ$5.5bn; return on capital 11.2%, tracking within the FY26 10-12% target range.
Sale of Mainland Group to Lactalis completed.

Record date (9 April) and payment date (14 April) for the tax-free NZ$2.00 per share/unit capital return (~NZ$3.2 billion group-wide) funded from Mainland divestment proceeds; combined with the imputed dividend, Fonterra distributed approximately NZ$3.9 billion in cash to shareholders and unit holders on 14 April 2026.

Fonterra Shareholders' Fund units delisted from the ASX (secondary listing), consolidating trading on the NZX Main Board only, to reduce dual-listing compliance/administrative costs and improve liquidity concentration.

Fonterra shifted emissions reporting basis to per kg Fat and Protein Corrected Milk (FPCM) from per kgMS, and continued a voluntary emissions-differentiated milk payment scheme (paying farmers 1-5 NZc/kgMS above baseline for lower-emissions milk from June 2025), in the absence of a government-mandated agricultural emissions price.

Fonterra Board chair Peter McBride publicly stated the co-operative has 'no appetite at this stage' to wind up the Fonterra Shareholders' Fund, addressing recurring investor speculation about the Fund's long-term future given the reduced (10%) size cap and the broader capital-structure simplification trend.

guidance.as_of: 1H FY2026 results (23 March 2026) / FY2025 Annual Report

items.notes: Raised from original 45-65 cents range (bottom end lifted) at the 1H FY2026 results, reflecting underlying business strength; excludes the divested Mainland Group and one-off divestment/separation costs.

Range narrowed and midpoint lifted from $9.50/kgMS ($9.20-$9.80 range) at 1H FY2026 results; a HIGHER milk price is a cost to the group and compresses Ingredients margins even as it benefits farmer-suppliers.
Tracking at 11.2% at 1H FY2026, within range; target unchanged even after the Mainland divestment per the September 2024 strategic targets.

items.target: up to 80% of earnings (top of policy range)
items.notes: FY2025 dividend of 57 cents/share represented 80% of normalised earnings, supported by strong balance sheet (net debt/EBITDA ~1.1x).
Forecast collections lifted at 1H FY2026 results on stronger-than-expected milk flows.

items.target: return to current (pre-divestment) earnings levels within ~3 years
items.notes: Qualitative target from CEO Miles Hurrell (FY2025 annual report) acknowledging near-term EPS/operating profit impact from losing Mainland Group earnings.

guidance.management_commentary: 1H FY2026 Chair Report (Mary Jane Daly): 'ongoing strength of Fonterra's performance,' Operating profit growth attributed to stronger in-market pricing and favourable product mix, particularly Foodservice benefiting from Southeast Asia and Greater China demand; management flagged Middle East conflict-related risks to input costs and shipping as the main outlook uncertainty. Outgoing CEO Miles Hurrell noted 'global demand for Fonterra's products continues to be strong' but flagged increasing global milk supply and FX/geopolitical volatility risk to commodity prices.

bull_case: Simplified, deleveraged, more focused co-operative post-Mainland divestment with net debt down to NZ$4.9bn, debt/EBITDA around 1.1x, and an 80%-of-earnings payout policy supporting strong, growing cash distributions to unit holders
Large one-off tax-free NZ$2.00/unit capital return (paid April 2026) plus rising interim/final dividends demonstrate substantial and growing capital-return capacity

Foodservice segment (Greater China, Southeast Asia) is growing rapidly (Q3 FY2026 underlying operating profit +143% YoY) and offers structurally higher, less-commoditised margins than pure Ingredients, with management targeting a return to pre-divestment group earnings within roughly three years
Return on capital tracking at 11.2%, within/above the 10-12% target range and ahead of Fonterra's 5-year average, alongside FY2026 guidance raised twice already this fiscal year
Dominant, largely unreplicable scale in NZ milk collection (~80-85% of national supply) provides a durable low-cost raw-material base underpinning global Ingredients and Foodservice competitiveness
bear_case: Fund unit holders have zero voting rights or governance influence at Fonterra; the co-operative board is legally and culturally obligated to maximise returns to farmer-suppliers (via the Farmgate Milk Price) ahead of Fund unit-holder profit interests — a structural conflict that cannot be resolved by unit holder action

Post-Mainland-divestment earnings are now more concentrated in commodity Ingredients and China/SE Asia Foodservice, both exposed to GDT price volatility, FX swings, and Chinese demand cycles, with less diversification than the previous branded-consumer-inclusive portfolio

The Fund's relative size cap was already cut from ~20% to 10% under 2023's Flexible Shareholding reform, the ASX secondary listing was voluntarily shed in 2025, and the buy-out pricing formula was already amended in 2024 — a clear multi-year trend of the Fund being marginalised within Fonterra's capital structure, even though a full wind-up has been explicitly (if only currently) ruled out by the Fonterra chair

High Farmgate Milk Price outcomes (good news for the ~8,000 farmer-owners who actually control Fonterra) mechanically compress the group margins and earnings that drive Fund unit holder returns — the two shareholder classes' interests are directly opposed on this single largest cost/revenue line

Leadership transition risk with CEO Miles Hurrell's departure (successor Richard Allen from ~September 2026) introduces execution uncertainty just as the co-operative integrates a major divestment and pursues a new post-Mainland growth strategy
sources_and_verification_notes: Financial figures and structural details sourced from Fonterra Shareholders' Fund Annual Reports FY2018-FY2025 and Interim Report H1-2026 (research/FSF.NZ/Extracted/), cross-checked against Fonterra Co-operative Group media releases and third-party financial press (Bloomberg, BusinessDesk, NZ Herald, Rural News Group, DairyReporter, foodingredientsfirst.com) via web search current to approximately August 2026. The August-2025 headline Lactalis deal value was reported at different points as both ~$3.845bn and $4.22bn in different sources/stages of the transaction (likely reflecting enterprise value vs. final consideration or FX/adjustment differences) -- $4.22bn is used as the figure most consistently cited at and after completion (31 March 2026) and is treated as authoritative here, but this discrepancy could not be fully reconciled from available sources and should be verified against Fonterra's FY2026 annual report once published. The exact current (August 2026) FSF unit price/market cap and specific date of the Fonterra chair's 'no appetite to wind up' comment could not be pinned to a single precise date from available search results and are flagged as directionally accurate but not independently verified against a primary source document in this research pass.
